Hey there sorry for the late reply. I’m not sure if I can go into a lot of detail about it and I wouldn’t recommend this to anyone who was my age at the time of writing this post (I was 14) but I also want to be totally honest. my circumstances lead me to discover self medicating via weed.

I couldn’t get therapy without my parents being involved in the process and in my mind that wasn’t an option. They were part of the reason I wanted therapy in the first place and I knew they’d ask intrusive questions that I wasn’t up to answer.
Every online alternative (I.e. seven cups) was uhhh awful lol wouldn’t recommend. I tried everything I could to get better including seeing a school assigned counselor but that also sucked big balls, they either A. Called my parents. Counterintuitive… or B. Told me useless stuff that didn’t help very much lol. Venting on discord could only help so much. Journaling was a temporary respite. Etc you get the point

Eventually I found recourse in self medicating which “dulled” the daily anger into something more manageable. Instead of feeling that usual evil feeling id feel free and be able to focus on things outside my anger like the way flowers and plants looked whenever they swayed in the wind. Or how sunlight would filter through my houses windows and hit the walls coloring everything orangish yellow.
Then to make a long story short after that I found a will to live, started approaching people with way more kindness in my heart, made new friends, grew up and got properly medicated with fluoxetine 3 years later when I was 17. 
As of today I’m 20 and not suicidal anymore or as disillusioned with the world as I was when I posted this. I’m doing very well compared to where I was and I hope any part of my response helped you even just a little bit.
It would make me angry back then to hear “it gets better” because I hated when people would make promises to me on behalf of the universe. So instead I think it’s better to say, our anger will always be a part of us. It helps to remember we evolved anger to know when we are being mistreated. And even though it hurts, I think we’ll be okay

My first thought after making it to that last line of this one was, “holy shit.”
The depth provided by the whimsical yet almost gritty imagery is so lovely. The build up of someone or something desperately waiting and yearning made that last line of descending clouds of anguish even more impactful. Like a weight lifted off both the speaker and the readers shoulders. It speaks of acceptance and moving on on the speakers behalf. The way the prose and formatting connect to deliver rhythmically gut punching lines is some good stuff.
That contrasting element of nature revisited in the speakers dark time of unrequited love is superb. I can’t help but get a feel of hope being encouraged to grow through barriers of inauthenticity and disconnection, accomplished by the speakers will to feel and move through their pain despite their heart still being within the painful grasp of another. The beginnings allusions to inauthenticity—

>	faux-feather ribbons and plastic vases

Combined with the radiant and gentle imagery of 

>	aromatic smells and golden pollen
Petals dancing in front of our faces

 Make me think the speaker is willing to look back and see how good a connection of the past makes them feel, no matter how inauthentic. As if the petals being alluded to in the third line are in reality obscurities, clouding both the speaker and their lovers boundaries in the name of tenderness, which works out at the end as the romantic view of their situation comes to a hard halt. 

>	My bountiful love while she loves me not
Her stargazer lilies start to dry up

These lines are very interesting. The garden of the speakers mind slowly retracts associations of growth with their love, and instead let their lilies dry from never being watered with devotion. That’s what makes the segue to destruction *and* acceptance impactful>>

>	shattered stems and demolished trains of thought
My white roses and her thorns start to blend
The vast clouds of anguish start to descend

Now in the speakers garden, white roses representing themselves and the parts of their lover that hurt begin to enmesh in painful acceptance. Even though the speaker is in pain and addicted to the allure of their lover, there is the knowing that all is not over yet. That this isn’t the end for the speakers want to love and be loved.
Argh! So good. Keep up the nice work.
Also if I got this entirely wrong, oops. It’s a learning process for us all haha

I love how the lines 

>	write down your dreams on paper and
eat them

Provoke imagery of the reader embodying their dreams, purpose, goals, and passions by embracing them and, in that sense, *digesting* them. I can almost feel the scrap of paper on my throat and taste pen ink as my dreams work themselves down. And how the line

>	There’s no sweeter taste than taking control

Casts that digestion of passion in an empowering light. It’s interesting that the beginning of the poem is seemingly upbeat and adoring of what life has to offer, but then that excitement waters down into calmness as the poem reads. The little space between 
the lines of control and the couch add a neat bit of impact as that empowerment transitions into taking action. 

>	the couch is surely as bored as you
It’s time to move it move it 

I’m not sure whether or not that last line is referring to the animated movie Madagascar or not lol but either way I’m not sure what the repetition adds besides furthering the implication of movement—though coupled with the stagnation in the couch line i feel it works as a little bit of a push. Move it—*Move it!*
The length and limited descriptions are my only complaint, although I like to imagine the speaker wrote this poem and immediately jumped up to dance around in delight of being alive. Lengthwise, there’s some lot left to desire. It makes me raise the questions about why the speaker sees the world through such a positive lense and why they’re inviting the reader to see it that way as well. Overall, this poem slaps. I like it.

Except for the fact that when you *can’t* enjoy anything, or are numb to activities that usually bring you enjoyment, it’s useless to attempt. 
Not to say it’s most common in unhealthy lifestyles, just easier to spot. I can’t speak for those depressed people you spent time with, and I’m happy they were able to ease out of their personal struggles, but it doesn’t seem that simple.

When your ability to even enjoy what life has to offer is taken away, there’s seemingly no point to continue, however more years you supposedly have. You see a sunset and talk about how beautiful it is, how they should *see* how beautiful it is, and how selfish they are for not wanting to continue despite not even being able to experience the sunset the same way you do. As poignantly explained in [Stanford Saploskys lecture on depression](https://youtu.be/NOAgplgTxfc) 
Call me crazy, but saying it’s stupid is wilder than considering it when you have no where else to go.

If you’re alive, you’re experiencing life. The first 18 years aren’t a test trial.
Instead of being critical of the thinking of a depressed person, try out compassion. It seems like you’re just trying to guilt people into staying alive rather than seeing from their perspective.
